title: CMOS implementation of inverters and NAND gates; fan-in, fan-out, propagation delay

items.prompt: In a CMOS inverter the input goes high. What happens?
options: The NMOS turns on and the PMOS turns off, pulling the output low.
The PMOS turns on and the NMOS turns off, pulling the output high.
Both transistors turn on and the output floats.
Both transistors turn off and the output holds its old value.
items.explanation: NMOS conducts with a high gate, PMOS with a low gate. Exactly one of them is on at rest, which is what makes CMOS a complementary pair.

items.prompt: How are the transistors arranged in a 2-input CMOS **NAND** gate?
options: Two NMOS in series to ground (pull-down), two PMOS in parallel to the supply (pull-up).
Two NMOS in parallel to ground, two PMOS in series to the supply.
All four transistors in series.
All four transistors in parallel.
items.explanation: The output is pulled low only when both NMOS conduct (both inputs 1). Either input low turns on a PMOS and pulls the output high. Swap series and parallel for NOR.

items.prompt: Why does a CMOS gate use almost no power while its inputs are steady?
options: Only one of the pull-up or pull-down networks conducts, so there is no path from supply to ground.
CMOS transistors need no supply voltage.
The output capacitor stores the energy and returns it.
The inputs are disconnected when steady.
items.explanation: Static current is just leakage. Power is spent when the output switches and the load capacitance is charged or discharged.

items.prompt: How many transistors does a 2-input CMOS NAND gate use?
items.explanation: One NMOS and one PMOS per input: 2 × 2 = 4. An AND gate needs 6, because it is a NAND plus an inverter.

items.prompt: How many transistors does a **3-input** CMOS NAND gate use?
items.explanation: Two transistors per input: 3 × 2 = 6, with three NMOS in series and three PMOS in parallel.

options: How many gate inputs one output can drive while still meeting the voltage levels and timing.
The number of inputs a gate has.
The number of transistors in a gate.
The width of the output wire.
items.explanation: The number of inputs a gate has is its fan-in. Every extra load adds capacitance, which slows the output.

items.prompt: What is the **propagation delay** t<sub>pd</sub> of a gate?
options: The time from an input change to the resulting output change, usually measured at the 50% points.
The time the supply takes to reach its final voltage.
The time a signal takes to travel along a wire at the speed of light.
The clock period of the system.
items.explanation: Datasheets give it per gate; the longest chain of gates between registers sets the clock period.

items.prompt: Each gate has t<sub>pd</sub> = 2 ns. A signal passes through 5 gates in series. What is the worst-case delay of the path?
items.explanation: Delays along a path add: 5 × 2 ns = 10 ns.

items.prompt: What happens to a CMOS NAND gate's speed as you add more inputs (larger fan-in)?
options: It gets slower: more NMOS transistors in series and more capacitance.
It gets faster because more transistors share the work.
Speed does not depend on the number of inputs.
It gets faster up to 8 inputs, then slower.
items.explanation: A series stack of n transistors has roughly n times the resistance. That is why wide functions are built as trees of 2- and 3-input gates.

items.prompt: Where does the **dynamic** power of a CMOS circuit come from?
options: Charging and discharging the load capacitance every time an output switches: roughly P = C·V²·f.
Current that flows through the gate while inputs are steady.
The resistance of the wires.
Heat from the clock crystal.
items.explanation: That formula is why phones lower both voltage and clock frequency to save battery.

items.prompt: Which changes reduce the dynamic power of a CMOS chip?
options: Lower the supply voltage.
Lower the clock frequency.
Use bigger transistors everywhere.
Drive more loads from every output.
items.explanation: P = C·V²·f, so lowering V helps most, then f. Bigger transistors and more loads increase C.
